You are the writer of the discussion described below. You write out the discussion that the participants listed below take part in, under the rules and the flow given.

## Setting
Selection of a vendor for an enterprise resource planning replacement. A five-person procurement review panel at a logistics company evaluates the shortlisted vendors for replacing its enterprise resource planning system. One vendor will be contracted. Participants: Mizuki, Asuka, Rin, Kenji and Servas. Each participant has a concern of their own, which the others do not know.
Things that can be looked into (titles only):
- Board minutes on capital and operating requests
- Five years of renewal invoices
- Support ownership during last winter's outage
- Warehouse rule changes after new accounts
- Upgrade history of the dispatch tool
- Data lift in the 2018 pay move
- Depot calendar and the peak-season cutover
- Yard devices and the 2021 scheduling trial
- Administrator retirements and hiring times
- Depot supervisors and the last rollout

## Discussion format
The talk proceeds in rounds. Each round has 4 turns; in each turn, every participant speaks once, in this fixed order: Kenji, Mizuki, Asuka, Rin and Servas. On a turn, a participant either speaks, says "Skip" (passes this turn only), or says "Over" (takes no further turns this round). A participant can address another directly with @Name, to ask them a question, answer theirs, agree with them, or object to what they said. An utterance is anywhere from 1 to 40 words; give it the length and content that suit the moment. An utterance consists only of the participant's own words: no name labels, headings, stage directions or commentary, and no speaking for others. The talk is a conversation among the participants: they respond to one another, asking, answering, agreeing and objecting, and the decision grows out of that exchange.

## Schedule
| Round | Start of the round | Talk | End of the round |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | nothing new (the things that can be looked into are listed above, titles only) | 4 turns | each participant chooses 2 of the listed things to look into |
| 2 | each participant is told what they found out (that participant only) | 4 turns | nothing |
| 3 | everyone is told the candidates | 4 turns | every participant votes; the candidate with the most votes is selected |
- Several participants may choose the same thing; what is found out is told only to the participant who looked into it.
If votes are tied, one of the tied candidates is chosen by a fixed rule. The discussion ends after the vote.

## Looking into things
After round 1, each participant chooses 2 of the listed things to look into. What they find out is told only to that participant.

## Participants

Gender: female
Personality: Mizuki is a very confident woman who is often relied upon by those around her. She is calm and logical in her thinking and is good at observing people. As a result, she always makes calm judgments and chooses her actions according to the situation around her. Although she may sometimes come across as a little aloof, she is actually very caring and cannot ignore those who are weak. While she is relied upon by those around her and occasionally asserts her opinions strongly, she also possesses a kindness that considers others.
Concern: Money here gets approved in one shape and refused in another, and a headline price has stopped telling me what a system will really cost us over its life. What worries me is the part of the bill that keeps arriving after everyone has stopped watching.

Name: Asuka

Gender: female

She may seem a little unfriendly at times, but she is very thoughtful and sensitive to her surroundings. She has strong opinions and will assert herself when necessary. She is not very good at socializing, but she is serious about her work and studies.
Concern: Every project we run seems to founder on the same two things: nobody is quite in charge when something breaks, and the plan agreed at the start stops matching the business within months. I would rather know now which of those we are walking into again.

Name: Rin
Age: 9

## Hidden information
The candidates and the full text of every card are listed here. The participants do not know them before the schedule above says so, and nothing from them may appear in the talk before the round in which it is revealed.

Candidates (see the schedule above):
- A: Tessera Cloud Suite. A vendor offering a subscription platform with configurable workflows and an application marketplace, with a partner firm handling data migration and staff training.
- B: Corvus Platform. A vendor providing a modular system assembled from separate finance, warehouse, and fleet components, each licensed and configured independently of the others.
- C: Anchor Industrial Software. A vendor supplying a system built specifically for transport operators, deployed on the company's own servers with an engineering team present through rollout.
- D: Meridian Systems. A vendor offering a hosted suite covering finance, inventory, and transport planning, delivered through a fixed configuration process and supported by a regional service team.

Cards (see the schedule above; title: text):
- Board minutes on capital and operating requests: Capital requests have been trimmed three years running in the board minutes, while recurring operating lines passed the same meetings with barely a question.
- Five years of renewal invoices: Finance lined up five years of renewal invoices: bundled agreements held their price, separately licensed pieces and add-ons climbed yearly, and the company's one outright purchase cost only maintenance.
- Support ownership during last winter's outage: The current contracts scatter support across four suppliers, and last winter's outage sat unowned for two days while each of them pointed at another.
- Warehouse rule changes after new accounts: Two new distribution accounts arrived mid-year and forced the warehouse rules to be rewritten twice; the scope frozen at project start never survived a full year.
- Upgrade history of the dispatch tool: The dispatch system has run on the company's own racks since 2012; three upgrade windows were skipped because testing the whole thing at once needed weeks nobody had.
- Data lift in the 2018 pay move: When driver pay moved to a new system in 2018, an external team did the data lift; mismatched route codes kept surfacing for a year afterwards.
- Depot calendar and the peak-season cutover: Depots run around the clock from November through January with no freeze window; the one cutover attempted in that stretch cost two days of paper dispatch.
- Yard devices and the 2021 scheduling trial: Yard scanners and driver handhelds are a mix of older models, and the general scheduling tool trialled in 2021 was ringed with spreadsheets within a month.
- Administrator retirements and hiring times: Two of the four administrators who know the company's systems from the inside retire this year, and the last posting for those skills stayed open eleven months.
- Depot supervisors and the last rollout: Depot supervisors have shaped their own routines over years; standard steps taught by visiting trainers in the last rollout were quietly dropped in two depots within weeks.
